## Supplementary Information

### Osmotic pressure of nematic liquid crystal solutions

To estimate the osmotic pressure of nematic liquid crystals (LCs) we use the expression [100]

$$ \Pi_{\mathrm{osm}}=3n_{\mathrm{p}}k_{\mathrm{B}}T, $$

where $n_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the number density of nematic liquid crystal molecules, $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is Boltzmann’s constant, and $T$ is the absolute temperature. We estimate the number density as $n_{\mathrm{p}}\approx 4\phi/(L^{2}D\pi)$ [100, 101], where $\phi$ is the fractional volume occupied by the LC particles, $D$ is the average diameter of the LC particles, and $l$ is the average length of the LC particles. Inputting the values of Table S1 renders $\Pi_{\mathrm{osm}}=$2000\text{\,}\mathrm{Pa}$$ .

### Estimation of chain distance from a surface

We observe that buckling occurs in chains that have at least one endpoint transiently pinned, suggesting that bacterial chains come into contact with the surfaces of the imaging device (the chain’s endpoints may come into contact with the glass bottom surface [102] or with the top PDMS surface [103]). To incorporate these surface effects into the theoretical calculations, we assume that the filament is growing a distance, $h$ , from a surface (Fig. S2). To estimate $h$ experimentally, we track the $z$ -coordinate of a chain’s endpoints throughout the experiment. Next, we calculate the standard deviation of the $z$ -coordinate time series. The standard deviation yields an estimate of the chain’s fluctuations near the surface of the imaging device, providing an estimate of a chain’s average distance from the surface. We repeated this procedure for multiple buckling chains. The averages of these measurements are shown in Table S1 for different DSCG concentrations.

## Mathematical modeling

### S5.4 Slender filament growth and kinematics

The bacterial chain will be treated as a continuum filament of length $L(t)$ , which starts at $t=0$ in a straight configuration with centerline $\bm{X}_{0}(S)$ parameterized by the arclength $S\in[-L(0)/2,L(0)/2]$ (the reference frame). At time $t$ , the centerline position is written as $\bm{x}_{0}(s(S,t),t)$ , where $s\in[-L(t)/2,L(t)/2]$ is the current arclength parameter and $|\partial_{s}\bm{x}_{0}|=1$ .

Assuming a uniform growth law for each unit of bacterial length, we have $\partial s/\partial S=\alpha$ and $\dot{s}\equiv\partial_{t}s(S,t)=\alpha s(S,t)$ . Hence, with $s(S,0)=S$ , we have naturally that $s(S,t)=S\exp(\alpha t)$ .

The material velocity, denoted by $\bm{V}(S,t)$ , of the filament centerline is given by the time rate of change of the current position for fixed material coordinate $S$ :

$$ \displaystyle\bm{V}(S,t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\bm{x}_{0}(s(S,t),t)\Big|_{S}=\partial_{t}\bm{x}_{0}\Big|_{s}+\dot{s}\,\partial_{s}\bm{x}_{0}\eqqcolon\bm{v}(s(S,t),t)+\alpha s(S,t)\bm{\hat{s}}(s(S,t),t), $$

where $\bm{\hat{s}}\equiv\partial_{s}\bm{x}_{0}(s(S,t),t)$ is the unit tangent vector along the centerline. We recognize the final two terms as the rigid body motion component and the growth component, respectively. We further decompose the rigid body motion into its tangential and normal parts. At time $t$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\bm{v}(s,t)=v_{\parallel}(s,t)\bm{\hat{s}}(s,t)+\bm{v}_{\perp}(s,t), $$

where $\bm{\hat{s}}\cdot\bm{v}_{\perp}=0$ . Continuity demands that $|\partial_{s}\bm{x}_{0}|=1$ at all times, which implies that

$$ \displaystyle 0=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}|\partial_{s}\bm{x}_{0}|^{2}=\partial_{s}\bm{x}_{0}\cdot\partial_{st}\bm{x}_{0}=\bm{\hat{s}}\cdot\partial_{s}(\partial_{t}\bm{x}_{0})=\bm{\hat{s}}\cdot\partial_{s}\bm{v}. $$

As expected, the rigid body component of the filament velocity must be constant in the tangential direction, $v_{\parallel}(s,t)=v_{\parallel}(t)$ , or else the filament would rupture.

### S5.5 Filament geometry

For a small planar displacement of the filament, $u$ , we write the centerline position as

$$ \displaystyle\bm{x}_{0}(s,t)=s\hat{\bm{x}}+u(s,t)\hat{\bm{y}}+\mathcal{O}(Lu_{s}^{2}), $$

where $\{\hat{\bm{x}},\hat{\bm{y}},\hat{\bm{z}}\}$ denote the unit Cartesian vectors, with $\hat{\bm{x}}$ pointing along the length of the undeformed filament. To study the initial instability we will assume that $|u_{s}|\ll 1$ . The centerline unit tangent vector, $\bm{\hat{s}}=\partial_{s}\bm{x}_{0}$ , is accompanied by normal and binormal unit vectors along the centerline, $\{\bm{\hat{n}},\hat{\bm{z}}\}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\hat{s}}=\hat{\bm{x}}+u_{s}\hat{\bm{y}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2}), \displaystyle\bm{\hat{n}}=-u_{s}\hat{\bm{x}}+\hat{\bm{y}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2}), $$

forming an orthonormal triad.

Each cross-section of the filament is assumed to be circular with diameter $2a$ . The filament surface, denoted by $\partial D$ (neglecting the filament ends), is then parameterized by $(s,\eta)\in[-L(t)/2,L(t)/2]\times[0,2\pi)$ , as

$$ \displaystyle\bm{x}(s,\eta)=\bm{x}_{0}(s)+a\hat{\bm{e}}_{\perp}(s,\eta), $$

where $\hat{\bm{e}}_{\perp}(s,\eta)=\cos\eta\,\bm{\hat{n}}(s)+\sin\eta\hat{\bm{z}}$ . At each point on the surface, $\bm{x}(s,\eta)\in\partial D$ , we have another orthonormal triad $\{\hat{\bm{\xi}},\hat{\bm{\zeta}},\bm{\hat{\nu}}\}$ , composed of two unit tangent vectors on the surface, $\hat{\bm{\xi}}=\bm{x}_{s}/\lvert\bm{x}_{s}\rvert$ and $\hat{\bm{\zeta}}=\bm{x}_{\eta}/\lvert\bm{x}_{\eta}\rvert$ , and the unit normal vector, which points into the LC, $\bm{\hat{\nu}}=\hat{\bm{\zeta}}\times\hat{\bm{\xi}}/\lvert\hat{\bm{\zeta}}\times\hat{\bm{\xi}}\rvert$ . With the centerline displacement assumed to be small, these are given by

$$ \displaystyle\bm{x}(s,\eta) \displaystyle=s\hat{\bm{x}}+a\hat{\bm{r}}+\mathcal{O}(Lu_{s}), \displaystyle\hat{\bm{\zeta}}(s,\eta) \displaystyle=-\sin\eta\bm{\hat{n}}(s)+\cos\eta\hat{\bm{z}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2}), \displaystyle\hat{\bm{\xi}}(s,\eta) \displaystyle=\bm{\hat{s}}(s)+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2}), \displaystyle\bm{\hat{\nu}}(s,\eta) \displaystyle=\cos\eta\bm{\hat{n}}(s)+\sin\eta\hat{\bm{z}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2}), $$

where $\hat{\bm{r}}(\eta)=\cos\eta\hat{\bm{y}}+\sin\eta\hat{\bm{z}}$ and $\bm{\hat{\eta}}(\eta)=-\sin\eta\hat{\bm{y}}+\cos\eta\hat{\bm{z}}$ are the radial and azimuthal coordinate vectors, respectively. Later we will use the fact that $\hat{\bm{\zeta}}=\bm{\hat{\eta}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})$ , $\bm{\hat{\nu}}=\hat{\bm{r}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})$ , and $\bm{\hat{s}}=\hat{\bm{x}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})$ , i.e. recovering cylindrical coordinates at leading-order.

### S5.6 Force balance and filament dynamics

Force balance is considered at each segment along the filament. At a station $s$ , in the limit of large viscous damping relative to the inertial effects (i.e., Stokes flow), the resultant force (per unit length) acting on the filament is zero at all times. We decompose this force as

$$ \displaystyle\bm{f}(s,t)=\bm{f}^{\text{viscous}}(s,t)+\partial_{s}\bm{F}(s,t)+\bm{f}^{\text{LC}}(s,t)=\bm{0}, $$

where $\bm{f}^{\text{viscous}}$ is the viscous drag, $\partial_{s}\bm{F}$ is the differential elastic force, and $\bm{f}^{\text{LC}}$ is the LC restoring force. We shall compute each of these terms in turn.

First is the viscous drag, which we model using a resistive force approximation,

$$ \displaystyle\bm{f}^{\text{viscous}}=-\bm{\mathcal{R}}\cdot\bm{V}, $$

where $\bm{\mathcal{R}}$ is a resistance tensor,

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\mathcal{R}}=\zeta_{\parallel}\bm{\hat{s}}\bm{\hat{s}}+\zeta_{\perp}(\bm{\mathrm{I}}-\bm{\hat{s}}\bm{\hat{s}}). $$

The drag coefficients $\zeta_{\parallel}$ and $\zeta_{\perp}$ penalize motion in the filament tangent and normal directions, respectively. In terms of the rigid body motion and growth components of the filament velocity, we may write

$$ \displaystyle\bm{f}^{\text{viscous}}=-\left[\zeta_{\parallel}\bm{\hat{s}}\bm{\hat{s}}+\zeta_{\perp}\left(\bm{\mathrm{I}}-\bm{\hat{s}}\bm{\hat{s}}\right)\right]\cdot\left(\bm{v}+\alpha s\bm{\hat{s}}\right)=-\zeta_{\parallel}(v_{\parallel}+\alpha s)\bm{\hat{s}}-\zeta_{\perp}\bm{v}_{\perp}. $$

For reference, in a Newtonian fluid with viscosity $\mu$ , we would have $\zeta_{\parallel}\approx 2\pi\mu/\log(L/2a)$ and $\zeta_{\perp}\approx 2\zeta_{\parallel}$ at leading-order in $1/\log(L/2a)$ , assumed small; or, we instead have $\zeta_{\parallel}\approx 2\pi\mu/\log(2h/a)$ and $\zeta_{\perp}\approx 2\zeta_{\parallel}$ if the filament is moving a distance $h\ll L$ away from a wall [80].

Next is the differential elastic force due to the connectivity of the filament itself. We assume that the filament cannot support a bending moment; hence, from the angular momentum balance, we can write the force density as a tangential piece alone, $\bm{F}(s,t)=T(s,t)\bm{\hat{s}}$ . With this, we can decompose the force balance, Eq. (9), into its tangential and normal components,

$$ \displaystyle-\zeta_{\parallel}(v_{\parallel}+\alpha s)+\partial_{s}T=0, \displaystyle-\zeta_{\perp}\bm{v}_{\perp}+(\bm{\mathrm{I}}-\bm{\hat{s}}\bm{\hat{s}})\cdot\left(\bm{f}^{\text{LC}}+T\partial_{s}\bm{\hat{s}}\right)=\bm{0}, $$

respectively, where we have used that $\bm{\hat{s}}\cdot\bm{f}^{\text{LC}}=0$ (see §S5.7). If both ends of the filament are free, the end tensions must equate, $T(\pm L/2)=T_{L}=\mathcal{O}(w^{2})$ , with $w=aW/K$ the dimensionless anchoring strength. Integrating the tangential force balance, Eq. (13a), thus yields $v_{\parallel}=0$ , as well as an expression for the tension,

$$ \displaystyle T(s,t)=T_{L}-\frac{\zeta_{\parallel}\alpha}{2}\left(\frac{L(t)^{2}}{4}-s^{2}\right). $$

This baseline tension can be negative (compression), which has the potential to buckle the filament. This compression can be even more pronounced if one end of the filament meets additional resistance, due to surface interactions, for instance.

Consider the extreme case when one endpoint (e.g., the one at $s=-L/2$ ) is pinned (hinged), which requires an additional tangential force $F$ there. With $\bm{V}(-L/2,t)=[v_{\parallel}(t)-\alpha L(t)/2]\hat{\bm{x}}+\bm{v}^{\perp}(-L/2,t)=\bm{0}$ , we find that $v_{\parallel}(t)=\alpha L/2$ and $\bm{v}^{\perp}(-L/2,t)=\bm{0}$ . Integrating (13a), we find that $-\zeta_{\parallel}\alpha L^{2}/2+T_{L}-T_{-L}=0$ for $T_{\pm L}\equiv T(\pm L/2)$ . Using the endpoint force balance, $F+T_{-L}=0$ , we find that the required tangential force is $T_{-L}=-F=T_{L}-\zeta_{\parallel}\alpha L^{2}/4$ . In this pinned problem the baseline tension is given instead by

$$ \displaystyle T(s,t)=T_{L}-\frac{\alpha\zeta_{\parallel}}{2}\left(\frac{L(t)}{2}-s\right)\left(\frac{3L(t)}{2}+s\right). $$

For the free filament, from (14), the tension is smallest (and becomes negative, as a compression) at the midpoint, $s=0$ . For the pinned filament, from (15) the tension is smallest at the point of pinning, $s=-L/2$ , and it can be up to 4 times larger in the absence of $T_{L}$ (i.e. $-\alpha\zeta L^{2}/8$ vs. $-\alpha\zeta L^{2}/2$ ).

In either case, using $\bm{v}_{\perp}=u_{t}\hat{\bm{y}}[1+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})]$ , Eq. (13b) may be written as

$$ \displaystyle\zeta_{\perp}u_{t}=T(s)u_{ss}+\hat{\bm{y}}\cdot\bm{f}^{\text{LC}}(s), $$

where $T(s)$ is given in Eq. (14), for free-free ends, or Eq. (15), for fixed-free ends. In the free-free case, the boundary conditions are selected to match the LC director field far away (assumed to be the $\hat{\bm{x}}$ -direction), i.e., $u_{s}(\pm L/2)=0$ . In the fixed-free case, the boundary conditions instead take the form $u(-L/2)=u_{s}(L/2)=0$ .

### S5.7 LC director field and traction

Before we can determine the traction on the filament due to the surrounding LC environment, we need to determine the LC configuration. Fortunately, the system is evolving slowly, so we can determine the LC field in a quasi-static manner, i.e., solving an equilibrium problem for each filament configuration. Here, we let $L=L(t)$ and drop all arguments of time since the LC director field is determined instantaneously at any given time $t$ .

Far from the bacterial chain, the LC director field is assumed to be uniform in the $\hat{\bm{x}}$ direction. Elsewhere, at a position $\bm{x}$ in the fluid, the LC director field is represented as $\bm{n}(\bm{x})=\hat{\bm{x}}+\bm{p}(\bm{x})+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2})$ with $\bm{p}\cdot\hat{\bm{x}}=\bm{0}$ , where $\bm{p}=\mathcal{O}(u_{s})$ in order to have a balance between the deflection and the director field. With this approximation, the Ericksen torque stress tensor and projected molecular field are given by

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\Pi}=K\nabla\bm{n}=K\nabla\bm{p}\left[1+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})\right], \displaystyle\bm{h}=\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{n})\cdot(\nabla\cdot\bm{\Pi})=K\nabla^{2}\bm{p}\left[1+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})\right], $$

respectively, for the single (Frank) elastic constant $K$ and projection operator $\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{n})\equiv\bm{\mathrm{I}}-\bm{n}\bm{n}$ , see Ref. [79]. At equilibrium, $\bm{h}=\bm{0}$ and so $\nabla^{2}\bm{p}=\bm{0}$ with $\bm{p}\to\bm{0}$ as $|\bm{x}|\to\infty$ . On the boundary, $\bm{x}\in\partial D$ , we have the projected surface molecular field

$$ \bm{h}_{\text{surf}}=\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{n})\cdot\left[\bm{\hat{\nu}}\cdot\bm{\Pi}-\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{\text{surf}}}{\partial\bm{n}}\right]=\left[K\partial_{\nu}\bm{p}-\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{n})\cdot\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{\text{surf}}}{\partial\bm{n}}\right]\left[1+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})\right], $$

where $\mathcal{F}_{\text{surf}}$ is a surface energy that describes how the director field is anchored to the bacteria (to be defined), see Ref. [104]. At equilibrium, $\bm{h}_{\text{surf}}(\bm{x})=\bm{0}$ for $\bm{x}\in\partial D$ . Note from Eq. (8a) that $\bm{h}_{\text{surf}}(\bm{x})=\bm{h}_{\text{surf}}(s\hat{\bm{x}}+a\hat{\bm{r}})+\mathcal{O}(u\nabla\bm{h}_{s})$ for $\bm{x}\in\partial D$ , so $\partial D$ is effectively a cylinder of radius $a$ aligned with $\hat{\bm{x}}$ . We thus introduce a cylindrical polar coordinate system $(s,r,\eta)\in[-L/2,L/2]\times[a,\infty)\times[0,2\pi)$ .

#### S5.7.1 Surface anchoring and director field

On the filament surface, the LC is assumed to satisfy weak (i.e. finite strength) degenerate tangential anchoring conditions, with surface energy

$$ \mathcal{F}_{\text{surf}}=\frac{W}{2}(\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\hat{\nu}})^{2}, $$

for the unit normal vector $\bm{\hat{\nu}}=\hat{\bm{r}}-u_{s}\cos\eta\hat{\bm{x}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2})$ and anchoring strength $W$ , see Ref. [105]. Since $\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\hat{\nu}}=\bm{p}\cdot\hat{\bm{r}}-u_{s}\cos\eta+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2})$ , the surface molecular field is

$$ \bm{h}_{\text{surf}}=\left[K\partial_{r}\bm{p}-W(\bm{p}\cdot\hat{\bm{r}}-u_{s}\cos\eta)\hat{\bm{r}}\right]\left[1+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})\right]. $$

Furthermore, since $\bm{p}\cdot\hat{\bm{x}}=0$ , we can write $\bm{p}=\phi_{1}(\bm{x})\hat{\bm{y}}+\phi_{2}(\bm{x})\hat{\bm{z}}$ , for two scalar functions $\phi_{1}=\mathcal{O}(u_{s})$ and $\phi_{2}=\mathcal{O}(u_{s})$ , which satisfy $\nabla^{2}\phi_{1}=\nabla^{2}\phi_{2}=0$ subject to $\phi_{1}(\bm{x}),\phi_{2}(\bm{x})\to 0$ as $|\bm{x}|\to\infty$ and

$$ \displaystyle K\partial_{r}\phi_{1}=W\left[(\phi_{1}-u_{s})\cos\eta+\phi_{2}\sin\eta\right]\cos\eta, \displaystyle K\partial_{r}\phi_{2}=W\left[(\phi_{1}-u_{s})\cos\eta+\phi_{2}\sin\eta\right]\sin\eta, $$

on $r=a$ .

#### Free-free case:

In the case of two free-filament ends, with $u_{s}(\pm L/2)=0$ , we can write $u$ as a cosine series:

$$ \displaystyle u(s,t)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\hat{u}_{k}(t)\cos\left(\frac{q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right), $$

where $q_{k}\equiv k\pi/2$ . Using separation of variables, we pose general series representations for $\phi_{1}$ and $\phi_{2}$ of the form:

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{1}(\bm{x}) \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{-2q_{k}\hat{u}_{k}}{L}\sin\left(\frac{q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right)\left[\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{K_{m}(2q_{k}r/L)}{K_{m}(2q_{k}a/L)}a_{k}^{m}e^{im\eta}\right], \displaystyle\phi_{2}(\bm{x}) \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{-2q_{k}\hat{u}_{k}}{L}\sin\left(\frac{q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right)\left[\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{K_{m}(2q_{k}r/L)}{K_{m}(2q_{k}a/L)}b_{k}^{m}e^{im\eta}\right], $$

where $K_{m}(\cdot)$ is the $m$ th modified Bessel function of the second kind and $a_{k}^{m}=\overline{a_{k}^{-m}}$ and $b_{k}^{m}=\overline{b_{k}^{-m}}$ are complex constants, which are to be determined now.

The boundary conditions on $r=a$ impose the conditions

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}e^{im\eta}\left[\frac{S_{k}^{m}}{w}a_{k}^{m}+\left(a_{k}^{m}\cos\eta+b_{k}^{m}\sin\eta\right)\cos\eta\right]=\cos^{2}\eta, \displaystyle\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}e^{im\eta}\left[\frac{S_{k}^{m}}{w}b_{k}^{m}+\left(a_{k}^{m}\cos\eta+b_{k}^{m}\sin\eta\right)\sin\eta\right]=\cos\eta\sin\eta, $$

where $w=aW/K$ is the dimensionless anchoring strength, $S_{k}^{m}=S_{m}(2q_{k}a/L)$ , and

$$ S_{m}(x)\equiv-\frac{xK_{m}^{\prime}(x)}{K_{m}(x)}. $$

Replacing the trigonometric functions with exponentials and evaluating coefficients yields the conditions

$$ \displaystyle 2a_{k}^{m}\left[1+\frac{2}{w}S_{k}^{m}\right]+a_{k}^{m-2}+a_{k}^{m+2}-ib_{k}^{m-2}+ib_{k}^{m+2}=2\delta_{0m}+\delta_{2m}+\delta_{-2m}, \displaystyle 2ib_{k}^{m}\left[1+\frac{2}{w}S_{k}^{m}\right]+a_{k}^{m-2}-a_{k}^{m+2}-ib_{k}^{m-2}-ib_{k}^{m+2}=\delta_{2m}-\delta_{-2m}. $$

where $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta function. Solving these recurrence relations yields $a_{k}^{m}=b_{k}^{m}=0$ for $m\notin\{-2,0,2\}$ , $b_{k}^{0}=0$ , $ib_{k}^{2}=ib_{k}^{-2}=a_{k}^{-2}=a_{k}^{2}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle a_{k}^{0}=\frac{S_{k}^{2}}{S_{k}^{0}+S_{k}^{2}+\frac{2}{w}S_{k}^{0}S_{k}^{2}},\quad\text{and}\quad a_{k}^{2}=\frac{S_{k}^{0}/2}{S_{k}^{0}+S_{k}^{2}+\frac{2}{w}S_{k}^{0}S_{k}^{2}}. $$

Altogether, we have the solution

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{1}(\bm{x}) \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{-2q_{k}\hat{u}_{k}}{L}\sin\left(\frac{q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right)\left[A_{k}\frac{K_{0}(2q_{k}r/L)}{K_{0}(2q_{k}a/L)}+B_{k}\cos(2\eta)\frac{K_{2}(2q_{k}r/L)}{K_{2}(2q_{k}a/L)}\right], \displaystyle\phi_{2}(\bm{x}) \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{-2q_{k}\hat{u}_{k}}{L}\sin\left(\frac{q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right)\left[B_{k}\sin(2\eta)\frac{K_{2}(2q_{k}r/L)}{K_{2}(2q_{k}a/L)}\right], $$

where

$$ A_{k}\equiv\frac{1/S_{0}(2q_{k}a/L)}{1/S_{2}(2q_{k}a/L)+1/S_{0}(2q_{k}a/L)+2/w}\quad\text{and}\quad B_{k}\equiv\frac{1/S_{2}(2q_{k}a/L)}{1/S_{2}(2q_{k}a/L)+1/S_{0}(2q_{k}a/L)+2/w}. $$

#### One free-end:

In the case of one fixed and one free-filament ends, with $u(-L/2)=0$ and $u_{s}(L/2)=0$ , respectively, we can instead write $u$ as the series

$$ \displaystyle u(s,t)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\hat{u}_{k}(t)\sin\left(\frac{Q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right), $$

for $Q_{k}\equiv(2k-1)\pi/4$ . In this case, we find

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{1}(\bm{x}) \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{2Q_{k}\hat{u}_{k}}{L}\cos\left(\frac{Q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right)\left[C_{k}\frac{K_{0}(2Q_{k}r/L)}{K_{0}(2Q_{k}a/L)}+D_{k}\cos(2\eta)\frac{K_{2}(2Q_{k}r/L)}{K_{2}(2Q_{k}a/L)}\right], \displaystyle\phi_{2}(\bm{x}) \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{2Q_{k}\hat{u}_{k}}{L}\cos\left(\frac{Q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right)\left[D_{k}\sin(2\eta)\frac{K_{2}(2Q_{k}r/L)}{K_{2}(2Q_{k}a/L)}\right], $$

where

$$ C_{k}\equiv\frac{1/S_{0}(Q_{k}2a/L)}{1/S_{2}(2Q_{k}a/L)+1/S_{0}(2Q_{k}a/L)+2/w}\quad\text{and}\quad D_{k}\equiv\frac{1/S_{2}(2Q_{k}a/L)}{1/S_{2}(2Q_{k}a/L)+1/S_{0}(2Q_{k}a/L)+2/w}. $$

#### S5.7.2 Surface traction

To compute the traction on the filament due to the LC, we will need the Ericksen stress tensor and the surface stress tensor, given by

$$ \displaystyle\bm{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{K}{2}\lVert\nabla\bm{n}\rVert^{2}\mathbf{I}-K\nabla\bm{n}\cdot\nabla\bm{n}^{T}, \displaystyle\bm{\mathrm{T}}_{\mathrm{surf}}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{surf}}\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{\hat{\nu}})-\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{\hat{\nu}})\cdot\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{surf}}}{\partial\bm{\hat{\nu}}}\bm{\hat{\nu}}, $$

respectively, see [79, 104].

The first part of the traction is associated with the Ericksen stress $\bm{\mathrm{T}}$ , and is given by $\bm{f}(s,\eta)=\bm{\hat{\nu}}\cdot\bm{\mathrm{T}}$ . But this traction enters at $\mathcal{O}(\bm{p}^{2})=\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2})$ , and so we neglect it. The second part of the traction is associated with the surface stress $\bm{\mathrm{T}}_{\mathrm{surf}}$ , and is given by $\bm{f}_{\mathrm{surf}}(s,\eta)=\nabla_{s}\cdot\bm{\mathrm{T}}_{\mathrm{surf}}$ , where $\nabla_{s}\equiv\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{\hat{\nu}})\cdot\nabla$ with $\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{\hat{\nu}})\equiv\bm{\mathrm{I}}-\bm{\hat{\nu}}\bm{\hat{\nu}}$ , a projection operator for the surface normal direction. Since $\bm{\bm{\hat{\nu}}}=\hat{\bm{r}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})$ , we note that

$$ \nabla_{s}=\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{\hat{\nu}})\cdot\nabla=\left(\hat{\bm{x}}\partial_{s}+\frac{1}{r}\bm{\hat{\eta}}\partial_{\eta}\right)\left[1+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})\right]. $$

For the weak degenerate tangential anchoring conditions considered above, we have the surface stress

$$ \bm{\mathrm{T}}_{\mathrm{surf}}=\frac{W}{2}(\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\hat{\nu}})^{2}\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{\hat{\nu}})-W(\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\hat{\nu}})\bm{\mathrm{P}}(\bm{\hat{\nu}})\cdot\bm{n}\bm{\hat{\nu}}, $$

for $\bm{\hat{\nu}}=\hat{\bm{r}}-u_{s}\cos\eta\hat{\bm{x}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2})$ and $\bm{n}=\hat{\bm{x}}+\phi_{1}\hat{\bm{y}}+\phi_{2}\hat{\bm{z}}+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2})$ . It follows that $\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\hat{\nu}}=(\phi_{1}-u_{s})\cos\eta+\phi_{2}\sin\eta+\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2})$ , and so,

$$ \bm{\mathrm{T}}_{\mathrm{surf}}=-W[(\phi_{1}-u_{s})\cos\eta+\phi_{2}\sin\eta]\hat{\bm{x}}\hat{\bm{r}}\left[1+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})\right]=-K\partial_{r}\left[\phi_{1}\hat{\bm{x}}\hat{\bm{y}}+\phi_{2}\hat{\bm{x}}\hat{\bm{z}}\right]\left[1+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})\right], $$

where we have used the boundary condition (20). Using (34) yields the surface traction:

$$ \bm{f}_{\mathrm{surf}}(s,\eta)=\nabla_{s}\cdot\bm{\mathrm{T}}_{\mathrm{surf}}=-K\left[\partial_{s}\partial_{r}\phi_{1}\hat{\bm{y}}+\partial_{s}\partial_{r}\phi_{2}\hat{\bm{z}}\right]\left[1+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})\right]. $$

Finally, the force (per length) acting on the filament at each station $s$ , i.e. $\bm{f}^{\mathrm{LC}}(s)$ , is found by integrating the total surface traction, $\bm{f}(s,\eta)+\bm{f}_{\mathrm{surf}}(s,\eta)$ , over the azimuthal angle, $\eta$ :

$$ \bm{f}^{\mathrm{LC}}(s)=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left[\bm{f}(s,\eta)+\bm{f}_{\mathrm{surf}}(s,\eta)\right]a\mathrm{d}\eta=-aK\left[\left(\int_{0}^{2\pi}\partial_{s}\partial_{r}\phi_{1}\mathrm{d}\eta\right)\hat{\bm{y}}+\left(\int_{0}^{2\pi}\partial_{s}\partial_{r}\phi_{2}\mathrm{d}\eta\right)\hat{\bm{z}}\right]\left[1+\mathcal{O}(u_{s})\right]. $$

Note that $\bm{\hat{s}}\cdot\bm{f}^{\mathrm{LC}}(s)=\mathcal{O}(u_{s}^{2})$ , as used earlier.

#### Two free ends:

For two free ends, we have from (28),

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{s}\partial_{r}\phi_{1} \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2q_{k}}{L}\right)^{2}\frac{\hat{u}_{k}}{a}\cos\left(\frac{q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right)\left[A_{k}S_{0}\left(\frac{2q_{k}a}{L}\right)+B_{k}\cos(2\eta)S_{2}\left(\frac{2q_{k}a}{L}\right)\right], \displaystyle\partial_{s}\partial_{r}\phi_{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2q_{k}}{L}\right)^{2}\frac{\hat{u}_{k}}{a}\cos\left(\frac{q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right)\Big[B_{k}\sin(2\eta)S_{2}\left(\frac{2q_{k}a}{L}\right)\Big], $$

on $r=a$ , for $q_{k}=\pi k/2$ . Using that $\cos(2\eta)$ and $\sin(2\eta)$ have zero mean, and inserting the expressions in (29), the LC restoring force is found to be

$$ \displaystyle\bm{f}^{\text{LC}}(s)\sim-\frac{16\pi aK}{L^{3}}\hat{\bm{y}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}q_{k}^{3}\hat{u}_{k}\left[\frac{4q_{k}a}{wL}-\frac{K_{0}(2q_{k}a/L)}{K_{0}^{\prime}(2q_{k}a/L)}-\frac{K_{2}(2q_{k}a/L)}{K_{2}^{\prime}(2q_{k}a/L)}\right]^{-1}\cos\left(\frac{q_{k}(2s+L)}{L}\right). $$

#### Fixed-free ends:

For only one free-end, the restoring force is similarly found to be (40), but with the substitutions $\cos\mapsto\sin$ and $q_{k}\mapsto Q_{k}=(2k-1)\pi/4$ .

### S5.8 Filament dynamics and buckling length estimates

The filament dynamics in Eq. (16) are now fully determined, and we can begin to analyze them. Let us at this stage non-dimensionalize the problem by defining a dimensionless time, $\tau\equiv\alpha t$ , dimensionless length, $\xi\equiv 2s/L(t)$ , where $\xi\in[-1,1]$ , and dimensionless displacement $U(\xi,\tau)\equiv u(s,t)/a$ . We also introduce the dimensionless filament length $\Lambda(\tau)\equiv L(t)/(2a)$ , dimensionless viscosity $\chi\equiv\zeta_{\perp}/\zeta_{\parallel}$ , dimensionless anchoring strength $w\equiv aW/K$ , and Ericksen number $\mbox{Er}\equiv a^{2}\zeta_{\parallel}\alpha/(2\pi K)$ .

From the uniform growth law, $L^{\prime}(t)=\alpha L(t)$ (see §S5.4), we have that

$$ \partial_{t}u(s,t)=a\alpha\left[\partial_{\tau}U(\xi,\tau)-\xi\partial_{\xi}U(\xi,\tau)\right], $$

and so the filament dynamics, i.e., Eq. (16), is governed by the dimensionless equation

$$ \chi(U_{\tau}-\xi U_{\xi})=\tilde{T}(\xi)U_{\xi\xi}+\mbox{Er}^{-1}F^{\mathrm{LC}}(\xi,\tau), $$

for the dimensionless tension

$$ \tilde{T}(\xi)\equiv\frac{T(s,t)}{\alpha\zeta_{\parallel}L(t)^{2}/4}=\begin{cases}-\left(1-\xi^{2}\right)/2&\text{free-free,}\\
-\left(1-\xi\right)\left(3+\xi\right)/2&\text{fixed-free,}\end{cases} $$

where we have dropped the end-force $T_{L}$ as lower order, the dimensionless LC restoring force

$$ \displaystyle F^{\mathrm{LC}}(\xi,\tau)\equiv\frac{f^{\mathrm{LC}}(s,t)}{2\pi K/a}=\begin{cases}-\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{q_{k}^{3}U_{k}}{\Lambda^{3}}\left[\frac{2q_{k}}{w\Lambda}-\frac{K_{0}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{0}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}-\frac{K_{2}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{2}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}\right]^{-1}\cos\left[q_{k}(1+\xi)\right]&\text{free-free,}\\
-\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{Q_{k}^{3}U_{k}}{\Lambda^{3}}\left[\frac{2Q_{k}}{w\Lambda}-\frac{K_{0}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{0}^{\prime}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}-\frac{K_{2}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{2}^{\prime}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}\right]^{-1}\sin\left[Q_{k}(1+\xi)\right]&\text{fixed-free,}\end{cases} $$

with $q_{k}=k\pi/2$ , $Q_{k}=(2k-1)\pi/4$ , and the Fourier series

$$ \displaystyle U(\xi,\tau)=\begin{cases}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}U_{k}(\tau)\cos\left[q_{k}(1+\xi)\right]&\text{free-free,}\\
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}U_{k}(\tau)\sin\left[Q_{k}(1+\xi)\right]&\text{fixed-free.}\end{cases} $$

with coefficients $U_{k}(\tau)\equiv u_{k}(t)/a$ .

#### S5.8.1 Two free-ends

In the free-free case, inserting the Fourier series for $U(\xi,\tau)$ and using the orthogonality of the basis functions yields

$$ \chi U_{k}^{\prime}(\tau)=\left\{\frac{\chi}{2}+\frac{q_{k}^{2}}{3}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{q_{k}^{3}}{\mbox{Er}\Lambda^{3}}\left[\frac{2q_{k}}{w\Lambda}-\frac{K_{0}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{0}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}-\frac{K_{2}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{2}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}\right]^{-1}\right\}U_{k}(\tau)+\sum_{m\neq k}J_{km}U_{m}(\tau), $$

for $q_{k}=\pi k/2$ and

$$ \begin{split}J_{km}&=\int_{-1}^{1}\left\{\frac{q_{m}^{2}}{2}(1-\xi^{2})\cos\left[q_{m}(1+\xi)\right]-\chi q_{m}\xi\sin\left[q_{m}(1+\xi)\right]\right\}\cos\left[q_{k}(1+\xi)\right]\mathrm{d}\xi\\
&=-[1+(-1)^{k+m}]\frac{m^{2}[m^{2}(1-\chi)+k^{2}(1+\chi)]}{(k^{2}-m^{2})^{2}},\end{split} $$

when $m\neq k$ . Here, we see that the even and odd modes about $\xi=0$ have uncoupled. Since there is fairly rapid decay in $k$ away from $k=m$ , a first approximation is to ignore the summation in Eq. (46). Doing this yields

$$ \chi U_{k}^{\prime}(\tau)\approx\left\{\frac{\chi}{2}+\frac{q_{k}^{2}}{3}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{q_{k}^{3}}{\mbox{Er}\Lambda^{3}}\left[\frac{2q_{k}}{w\Lambda}-\frac{K_{0}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{0}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}-\frac{K_{2}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{2}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}\right]^{-1}\right\}U_{k}(\tau). $$

Although $\Lambda(\tau)$ is generally time-dependent, to find the buckling lengths, we shall freeze it at its instantaneous value, $\Lambda(\tau)=\Lambda$ , and pose the ansatz $U_{k}(\tau)=e^{\sigma_{k}\tau}\hat{U}_{k}$ , yielding the growth rate of the $k$ th mode:

$$ \sigma_{k}\approx\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{\chi}\left\{\frac{q_{k}^{2}}{3}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{q_{k}^{3}}{\mbox{Er}\Lambda^{3}}\left[\frac{2q_{k}}{w\Lambda}-\frac{K_{0}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{0}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}-\frac{K_{2}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{2}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}\right]^{-1}\right\}. $$

It follows that the $k$ th mode becomes unstable when $\Lambda>\Lambda_{k}$ where $\Lambda_{k}$ solves

$$ \frac{\chi}{2}+\frac{q_{k}^{2}}{3}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{q_{k}^{3}}{\mbox{Er}\Lambda_{k}^{3}}\left[\frac{2q_{k}}{w\Lambda_{k}}-\frac{K_{0}(q_{k}/\Lambda_{k})}{K_{0}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda_{k})}-\frac{K_{2}(q_{k}/\Lambda_{k})}{K_{2}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda_{k})}\right]^{-1}\approx 0. $$

For small Er (and thus large $\Lambda_{k}$ ), we note that

$$ \frac{\Lambda_{k}^{3}}{q_{k}^{3}}\left[\frac{2q_{k}}{w\Lambda_{k}}-\frac{K_{0}(q_{k}/\Lambda_{k})}{K_{0}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda)}-\frac{K_{2}(q_{k}/\Lambda_{k})}{K_{2}^{\prime}(q_{k}/\Lambda_{k})}\right]=\frac{\Lambda_{k}^{2}}{2q_{k}^{2}}\left(1-2\gamma+\frac{4}{w}+\log\frac{4\Lambda_{k}^{2}}{q_{k}^{2}}\right)+\mathcal{O}\left(1\right), $$

as $q_{k}/\Lambda_{k}\to 0$ , where $\gamma$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant. At leading-order in $\mbox{Er}^{-1}$ , assumed large, we have that

$$ \frac{\Lambda_{k}^{2}}{2q_{k}^{2}}\left(1-2\gamma+\frac{4}{w}+\log\frac{4\Lambda_{k}^{2}}{q_{k}^{2}}\right)\approx\frac{4\mbox{Er}^{-1}}{2\chi-1+4q_{k}^{2}/3}, $$

which finally gives the approximation

$$ \Lambda_{k}\approx\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}k^{2}\mbox{Er}^{-1}}{2\chi-1+\pi^{2}k^{2}/3}\right)^{1/2}\left[W\left(\frac{32\mbox{Er}^{-1}e^{1-2\gamma+4/w}}{2\chi-1+\pi^{2}k^{2}/3}\right)\right]^{-1/2}, $$

where $W(z)$ is the Lambert $W$ function (the solution to $W\exp W=z$ ). Using the rudimentary approximation of $W(z)\approx\log z$ for large $z$ , this expression can be approximated further as

$$ \Lambda_{k}\approx\left(\frac{2\pi^{2}k^{2}\mbox{Er}^{-1}}{2\chi-1+\pi^{2}k^{2}/3}\right)^{1/2}\left[\log\left(\frac{32\mbox{Er}^{-1}}{2\chi-1+\pi^{2}k^{2}/3}\right)+1-2\gamma+\frac{4}{w}\right]^{-1/2}. $$

The buckling length of the filament is then given by the smallest critical length, $\Lambda^{*}=\min_{k}\Lambda_{k}$ . For $\chi=5$ , $\mbox{Er}=10^{-6}$ , and $w=10^{-2}$ – $10^{0}$ , we find that the smallest mode is $k=1$ , which gives the estimate to dimensionless buckling $\Lambda^{*}\approx 62.2$ – $294$ . This approximation is compared to numerical solutions of the coupled system, Eq. (46), in the main text Fig. 5. Although the numerical results are not quantitatively recovered, the approximation does recover the qualitative behavior. It thus inspires the fitting expression presented in the main text:

$$ \Lambda^{*}=\left(\frac{a_{1}\mbox{Er}^{-1}}{\log(a_{2}\mbox{Er}^{-1})+4/w}\right)^{1/2}, $$

for fitting parameters $a_{i}$ .

#### S5.8.2 Fixed-free ends

In the fixed-free case, inserting the Fourier series for $U(\xi,\tau)$ and using the orthogonality of the basis functions yields a similar expression to before:

$$ \chi U_{k}^{\prime}(\tau)=\left\{\frac{4Q_{k}^{2}}{3}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{Q_{k}^{3}}{\mbox{Er}\Lambda^{3}}\left[\frac{2Q_{k}}{w\Lambda}-\frac{K_{0}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{0}^{\prime}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}-\frac{K_{2}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{2}^{\prime}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}\right]^{-1}\right\}U_{k}(\tau)+\sum_{m\neq k}I_{km}U_{m}(\tau), $$

for $Q_{k}=\pi(2k-1)/4$ and

$$ \begin{split}I_{km}&=\int_{-1}^{1}\left\{\frac{Q_{m}^{2}}{2}(1-\xi)(3+\xi)\sin\left[Q_{m}(1+\xi)\right]+\chi Q_{m}\xi\cos\left[Q_{m}(1+\xi)\right]\right\}\sin\left[Q_{k}(1+\xi)\right]\mathrm{d}\xi\\
&=-\frac{(-1)^{k+m}(2m-1)^{2}\left[(2k-1)^{2}+(2m-1)^{2}\right]}{8(k-m)^{2}(k+m-1)^{2}}-\frac{(2m-1)\left[2k-1+(-1)^{k+m}(2m-1)\right]\chi}{4(k-m)(k+m-1)},\end{split} $$

when $m\neq k$ .

Again, omitting the summation in Eq. (56) and taking the ansatz $U_{k}(\tau)=e^{\sigma_{k}\tau}\hat{U}_{k}$ yields an approximation for the growth rate of the $k$ th mode,

$$ \sigma_{k}\approx\frac{1}{\chi}\left\{\frac{4Q_{k}^{2}}{3}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{Q_{k}^{3}}{\mbox{Er}\Lambda^{3}}\left[\frac{2Q_{k}}{w\Lambda}-\frac{K_{0}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{0}^{\prime}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}-\frac{K_{2}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}{K_{2}^{\prime}(Q_{k}/\Lambda)}\right]^{-1}\right\}. $$

For small Er, making the same approximations as before yields the fact that the $k$ th mode becomes unstable when $\Lambda>\Lambda_{k}$ , where

$$ \Lambda_{k}\approx\left(\frac{(2k-1)^{2}\pi^{2}\mbox{Er}^{-1}/2}{\pi^{2}(2k-1)^{2}/3-1}\right)^{1/2}\left[W\left(\frac{32\mbox{Er}^{-1}}{\pi^{2}(2k-1)^{2}/3-1}e^{1-2\gamma+4/w}\right)\right]^{-1/2}, $$

or, with the additional rudimentary approximation,

$$ \Lambda_{k}\approx\left(\frac{(2k-1)^{2}\pi^{2}\mbox{Er}^{-1}/2}{\pi^{2}(2k-1)^{2}/3-1}\right)^{1/2}\left[\log\left(\frac{32\mbox{Er}^{-1}}{\pi^{2}(2k-1)^{2}/3-1}\right)+1-2\gamma+\frac{4}{w}\right]^{-1/2}. $$

For $\chi=5$ , $\mbox{Er}=10^{-6}$ , and $w=10^{-2}$ – $10^{0}$ , here the smallest value of $\Lambda_{k}$ is found to range between when $k=6$ (for $w=10^{-2}$ ) and $k=2$ (for $w=10^{0}$ ), giving the estimate to dimensionless buckling $\Lambda^{*}\approx 60.5$ – $296$ . An improved estimation is found by fitting (55) to the coupled system, as presented in the main text.
